headline: The Cardiology Foundation
threshold: By Lesson 10, you can greet a patient, give a pulse and blood pressure, ask simple questions about pain, give polite instructions, ask for an interpreter, and start Cardiology Lesson 1.

lessons.title: Sounds and Greetings
lessons.objective: Greet a patient, say who you are, and pronounce basic heart and body words clearly.
lessons.focus: The five pure vowels, ch, j, ll, rr and the written accent, plus formal greetings

words.note: The written accent marks the stressed syllable: co-ra-ZÓN.
ch sounds like the ch in church.
Vowels are short and pure: a as in father, o as in no.
h is silent; j sounds like a strong English h.
rr is a strong trill: tap the tongue several times.
Stress MÉ-di-co. A woman is la médica.
A single r between vowels is a quick tap. A man is el enfermero.
ll sounds like English y in most of Mexico: ca-MI-ya.
A woman is la paciente. Say every vowel: pa-SYEN-te.
ñ sounds like ny in canyon. Polite way to address an adult woman.

words.es: Buenos días, soy la doctora Ruiz.
words.note: A male doctor says soy el doctor Ruiz.
Usted is the respectful form for patients.

words.en: Good afternoon, what is your name?

words.es: Hasta luego, que le vaya bien.
words.note: Common polite goodbye in Mexico.

lessons.speaking: Greet a patient at the bedside, say your name and role, and ask how they are today.

lessons.title: Numbers, Time and Measurements
lessons.objective: Say a patient's pulse, blood pressure, weight, room number and appointment time.
lessons.focus: Numbers 0 to 1,000, clock time, and pulse, pressure, pounds and mg with de

words.note: Short for la presión arterial.
Written mg on labels; say miligramos.

words.en: Your pulse is 72 beats per minute.
words.es: Su pulso es de 72 latidos por minuto.
words.note: Use de before a measurement.
Sobre means over, as in 130/80.

words.en: Your appointment is Tuesday at 9 in the morning.
words.es: Su cita es el martes a las 9 de la mañana.
words.note: Use a la for 1 o'clock and a las for other hours.
Add y media for half past: las 3 y media.

lessons.speaking: Tell a patient their pulse, blood pressure and weight, then give the day and time of their next appointment.

lessons.title: Ser and Estar
lessons.objective: Say who someone is and describe how a patient feels: stable, dizzy, tired or calm.
lessons.focus: ser for identity and role, estar for a patient's condition or location

words.note: A woman says mareada.
A woman says cansada.
A woman says nerviosa.
Un dolor fuerte is a severe pain.
A woman is la cardióloga.

words.es: El doctor López es su cardiólogo.
words.note: ser: who someone is or their role.
estar: a condition that can change.

words.en: The nurse is in the room.
words.es: La enfermera está en el cuarto.
words.note: estar for location.

lessons.speaking: Introduce the patient's cardiologist and ask the patient if they are dizzy, tired or nervous.

lessons.title: Have, There Is, Need and Want
lessons.objective: Ask what a patient has, needs or wants, and say what must be done next.
lessons.focus: tener, hay, necesitar, querer, and hay que + infinitive for what must be done

words.note: Common in Mexico; also la manta.
Feminine noun that takes el: el agua fría.

words.en: Do you want to call your family?
words.note: Use a before people as the object of a verb.

words.en: There is a bathroom in your room.
words.es: Hay un baño en su cuarto.

words.en: We need to do a blood test.
words.es: Hay que hacer un análisis de sangre.
words.note: Hay que + infinitive: something must be done.

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient if they have chest pain, if they need a blanket, and if they want to call their family.

lessons.title: Go, Do and Can
lessons.objective: Tell a patient where they are going and what you will do, and ask what they can do.
lessons.focus: ir, ir a + infinitive for plans, hacer, and poder + infinitive

words.note: Mexican and US usage.
Many people also say los rayos X.

words.en: We're going to the lab now.
words.note: a + el contracts to al.

words.en: Tomorrow you are going to go home.
words.es: Mañana va a ir a su casa.

words.en: We are going to do a chest X-ray on you.
words.es: Le vamos a hacer una radiografía del pecho.

words.en: Your family can wait in the waiting room.
words.es: Su familia puede esperar en la sala de espera.

lessons.speaking: Tell a patient you are going to do a chest X-ray, and ask if they can walk to the elevator.

lessons.title: Present Tense
lessons.objective: Ask about daily habits like smoking, salt and meals using present-tense verbs.
lessons.focus: Regular -ar, -er, -ir endings for yo, tú, usted, nosotros and ellos

words.note: Masculine despite ending in -a.
fumar: fumo, fumas, fuma, fumamos, fuman.

words.en: Do you eat a lot of salt?
Do you live alone or with your family?
words.note: Ask a woman: ¿Vive sola?

words.en: We'll talk with your daughter later.
words.es: Nosotros hablamos con su hija después.
words.note: The present tense often covers the near future.

words.en: The nurses take your blood pressure at night.
words.es: Las enfermeras toman su presión en la noche.

words.en: Are you writing the note, or should I?
words.es: ¿Tú escribes la nota o la escribo yo?
words.note: Informal tú with a coworker; use usted with patients.

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient if they smoke, eat a lot of salt and live alone, then ask a coworker who writes the note.

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.objective: Ask the basic questions: where it hurts, when it started, and which medicines they take.
lessons.focus: Question words qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cuánto, cómo, por qué, cuál

words.note: Plural: ¿quiénes?
Agrees with the noun: cuánta, cuántos, cuántas.
The answer porque, one word, means because.
Use cuál before es for names, numbers and dates.
doler works like gustar: me duele, le duele.

words.en: What is your date of birth?
words.note: Ask it to verify the patient's identity.

words.en: Why did you come to the hospital today?

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient where it hurts, when the pain started, what it is like, and what medicines they take.

lessons.title: No, Never and How Much
lessons.objective: Say no, never, nobody and not yet, and ask if a patient needs more or another thing.
lessons.focus: no, nunca, nadie, nada, todavía no, más, menos and otro; double negatives

words.note: otra for feminine nouns; never say un otro.

words.en: Don't you have anyone at home?
words.note: Spanish uses double negatives: no + nadie.

words.en: We don't have the results yet.
Never stop taking your pills without talking to your doctor.
words.es: Nunca deje de tomar sus pastillas sin hablar con su médico.

lessons.speaking: Tell a patient the results are not ready yet, and ask if they need another pillow or have more questions.

lessons.title: Polite Requests and Commands
lessons.objective: Ask a patient politely to sit, lie down, breathe deeply and put on a gown.
lessons.focus: ¿Puede + infinitive? and usted commands, with -se attached (siéntese, acuéstese)

words.note: Feminine despite ending in -o.

words.en: Can you put on the gown, please?
words.note: ¿Puede + infinitive? is a polite request.

words.en: Sit on the exam table, please.
words.es: Siéntese en la camilla, por favor.
words.note: Usted command of sentarse; -se attaches to the end.

words.en: Lie down on your left side.

words.note: hondo means deep.

words.en: Press the call button if you need anything.
words.es: Toque el timbre si necesita algo.

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient to put on the gown, sit on the stretcher, lie on their left side and breathe deeply.

lessons.title: Words You Already Know and Getting Help
lessons.objective: Recognize cognates and use survival phrases to slow down, repeat, or call an interpreter.
lessons.focus: Cognates ending in -ción, -dad and -ente, and survival phrases for getting help

words.note: English -tion becomes -ción; these words are feminine.
English -ty becomes -dad; these words are feminine.
English -ent becomes -ente.
A woman is la intérprete. Use a qualified interpreter for consent.

words.en: How do you say this in Spanish?
I'm going to call an interpreter.
words.es: Voy a llamar a un intérprete.
words.note: Use a before a person as the object.

lessons.speaking: Tell a patient you speak a little Spanish, ask them to repeat more slowly, and say you will call an interpreter.
